reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: An acquired immune-mediated demyelinating neuropathy defined by a progressive or relapsing course evolving over at least two months, distinguishing it from Guillain-Barre syndrome
Typically produces symmetrical proximal and distal weakness with large-fibre sensory loss, and reduced or absent reflexes
Unlike most axonal neuropathies, both proximal and distal muscles are affected, and weakness often dominates over sensory symptoms
Nerve conduction studies show demyelinating features: conduction slowing, conduction block, temporal dispersion, and prolonged distal latencies
Cerebrospinal fluid usually shows raised protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation)
Responds to immunotherapy including corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and plasma exchange, unlike axonal neuropathies
Several variants exist, including multifocal (Lewis-Sumner) and pure sensory or motor forms
Should prompt screening for associated conditions such as monoclonal gammopathy, diabetes, HIV, and lymphoma
reference.pathophysiology: CIDP is an autoimmune disorder in which cell-mediated and humoral responses target components of peripheral nerve myelin and Schwann cells, producing segmental demyelination and remyelination with characteristic onion-bulb formation on biopsy. Inflammatory infiltration occurs around endoneurial vessels and nerve roots. Demyelination slows or blocks conduction, causing weakness and sensory loss; secondary axonal degeneration accumulates over time and correlates with fixed deficits. A subset has antibodies against nodal or paranodal proteins (e.g. neurofascin, contactin), which behave somewhat differently and may respond poorly to immunoglobulin.
additionalDifferentials: Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute, monophasic course under 4 weeks)
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
Paraproteinaemic neuropathy including anti-MAG and POEMS syndrome
Diabetic polyneuropathy or diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm demyelinating physiology
Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid protein and cell count
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation for monoclonal protein
Nodal/paranodal antibody testing (neurofascin-155, contactin-1, CASPR1) in atypical or treatment-resistant cases
MRI of nerve roots and plexus showing hypertrophy or enhancement in selected cases
Nerve biopsy reserved for diagnostically uncertain presentations
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness threatening ambulation or respiratory or bulbar function
Features suggesting an underlying malignancy or POEMS syndrome such as weight loss, organomegaly, or skin change
Poor or absent response to first-line immunotherapy prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
Superimposed acute deterioration requiring differentiation from an axonal or systemic process
reference.prognosis: Most patients respond to immunotherapy and many achieve remission or long-term stabilisation, though the disease is often chronic and relapsing; delayed treatment allowing secondary axonal loss predicts greater residual disability.
pitfalls: Confusing a slowly evolving CIDP with Guillain-Barre syndrome and stopping treatment prematurely
Over-diagnosing CIDP in length-dependent axonal neuropathies that will not respond to immunotherapy
Missing an associated paraprotein or POEMS syndrome that changes management
Failing to recognise nodopathy variants that respond poorly to immunoglobulin
Not objectively documenting treatment response, leading to prolonged ineffective immunotherapy
management: First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
Maintenance immunoglobulin, including subcutaneous administration, or steroid-sparing immunosuppressants for relapsing or chronic disease
Treatment tailored for nodal and paranodal antibody-associated disease with rituximab, since these cases respond poorly to immunoglobulin
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and orthoses to maintain function and manage residual deficits
Monitoring of response and disability with serial nerve conduction studies to detect relapse and secondary axonal loss
Early treatment to limit axonal degeneration and fixed disability, under neurology specialist follow-up
